answer.label: Not Mother Teresa’s words — an unsourced paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1910–1997 · Roman Catholic nun & missionary, founder of the Missionaries of Charity
answer.sourceLine: The Mother Teresa Center ↗ — the official custodian of her words, run by her own order — lists this exact sentence among quotations that are “significantly paraphrased versions or personal interpretations” and expressly “not her authentic words.” The sentiment is broadly consistent with her teaching on not judging, but no book, speech, letter, or interview has ever been shown to contain this wording; it was removed from Wikiquote in 2009 ↗ as unsourced and remains undocumented.

source.excerpt: If you judge people, you have no time to love them.
trail: The Mother Teresa Center ↗, run by the Missionaries of Charity, lists this line among quotes that are paraphrases or personal interpretations and “not her authentic words.”
The fact-checking blog Fauxtations ↗ labels it a “fauxtation,” noting it was removed from Wikiquote in 2009 as unsourced and that no source has since been supplied.
On Wikiquote ↗ the line survives only with a hyperlink to a school blog — no book, page, speech, or date — the hallmark of an undocumented attribution.
Quote-aggregator pages such as Goodreads ↗ repeat the line with no citation, which is how the misattribution propagates.
source.excerptNote: The line spreads on social media, quote-aggregator sites, and greeting-card graphics — almost always with no source beyond “Mother Teresa.” Her own order asks that it not be presented as her authentic words.

author.heading: About Mother Teresa
author.metaLine: 1910–1997 · Catholic nun, missionary & Nobel Peace laureate
author.bio: Mother Teresa (born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu in Skopje) founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta in 1950 and spent decades serving the destitute and dying. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and was canonized as Saint Teresa of Calcutta in 2016. Her authentic words survive in works such as A Simple Path and No Greater Love and in her Nobel lecture — but her own order’s quote-verification effort shows how many feel-good lines were later pinned on her without any such source.

misattribution.heading: Why this one is flagged
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook feel-good misattribution: a warm, tidy aphorism pinned on a beloved figure with no documented source. What makes it unusual is that Mother Teresa’s own order has publicly disowned it.

items.why: No book, speech, letter, interview, or diary by Mother Teresa has ever been shown to contain this sentence. The Mother Teresa Center ↗ classifies it as a paraphrase or personal interpretation and states plainly it is “not her authentic words.”
It was removed from Wikiquote in 2009 ↗ as unsourced, and no one has produced a source in the years since. Its survival on aggregator sites rests entirely on repetition, not evidence.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea — that judging leaves no room for love — is broadly in keeping with Mother Teresa’s teaching, but this exact sentence is an undocumented paraphrase her own Center ↗ asks people not to present as her words.

context.heading: How a paraphrase becomes a “quote”
lead: Mother Teresa is one of the internet’s most frequent magnets for invented inspiration. Because she genuinely preached against judgment and for love of the outcast, a neatly balanced line like this “sounds right” — which is exactly why it sticks even without a source.

Her order took the unusual step of publishing a list of quotations wrongly credited to her, sorted into outright fabrications and softer paraphrases. This line sits in the paraphrase bucket: not a malicious fake, but not something she is documented to have said or written in these words.
detailsBody: A reliable tell of misattribution: the “citation” is always just the famous name. Search for a page number, a speech date, or a letter and you find nothing — only more images and aggregator entries repeating each other.
context.pull: Her own order publishes a list of things she never actually said. This line is on it.
